concepts.title: Progressive overload
concepts.hook: A heavy school bag can feel normal after a few weeks of carrying it. The bag did not change. What did?
concepts.rule: Muscles adapt to work they are not used to. To keep progressing, add weight, clean reps or training days, and keep each weekly jump small next to what you already do.

claims.text: Resistance work can build strength; a rising challenge can support further progress over time.
Strength work asks muscles to do more than they are used to. This is called overload.
Strength grows over time when the weight or the number of training days goes up.
The size of each week's rise, next to what you already do, is linked to injury risk.

items.stem: Asking your muscles for more work than they are used to has a name: ___.

options.feedback: This is the word the guide uses for making muscles do more than they are used to.
A warm-up is the easy start before the main work. More than usual is overload.
A cool-down is the easy end of a session. Asking for more than usual is overload.

items.stem: In her hostel room, Tara has done the same 10 squats every day for two months. What will she likely notice?

options.text: They feel much easier than at the start.
options.feedback: Her legs adapted to the work, so the same 10 squats now take less effort.
The same work tends to feel easier over time, as the body adapts to it.

options.text: They feel exactly as hard as day one.
options.feedback: Two months of the same work gives the body time to adapt, so it feels easier.

items.stem: Why do push-ups count as strength work even though they use no weights?

options.text: Body weight makes the muscles work hard.
options.feedback: The guide lists push-ups, pull-ups and planks as strength work that uses body weight as the load.

options.text: Only machines and weights can load a muscle.
options.feedback: Body weight is a load too. The guide counts push-ups as muscle work.
Push-ups make the arm and chest muscles work against body weight, so they count as muscle work.

items.stem: At the college gym, Dev's 8 kg rows feel easy now. Which change adds clean work?

options.text: Try 9 kg with the same good form.
options.feedback: A small jump in weight with good form gives his back a new task to adapt to.

options.text: Jump to 20 kg and swing the weight.
options.feedback: A huge jump that needs swinging is not clean work. Small rises keep form steady.

options.text: Keep 8 kg and do fewer reps.
options.feedback: Fewer reps at the same weight is less work, so it will not push him further.

items.stem: A friend says the only way to progress is heavier weight. What is missing?

options.text: More training days also build strength.
options.feedback: The guide links both heavier weight and more training days each week to stronger muscles.

options.text: Weight has nothing to do with strength.
options.feedback: Heavier weight does build strength. It is just not the only way to add work.

options.text: Lighter weight always builds more strength.
options.feedback: For strength, heavier loads tend to help more. Weight is simply not the only lever.

items.stem: In progressive overload, Neha adds 1 kg each month to a 10 kg lift. About what will she lift after 6 months?

options.feedback: Six months of 1 kg each adds 6 kg, so 10 plus 6 makes 16 kg.
That multiplies 10 by 6. She adds only 1 kg a month, so 6 kg in all.
That counts one month only. Six rises of 1 kg add 6 kg in total.

items.stem: Two runners each add 30 minutes next week. Who takes the bigger jump?

options.text: Asha, who now runs 60 minutes a week.
options.feedback: 30 on top of 60 is a 50% rise, while 30 on 300 is only 10%.

options.text: Om, who now runs 300 minutes a week.
options.feedback: Om adds the same 30 minutes, but on 300 that is just a 10% rise.
The minutes match, but the share differs. 30 is half of 60 but a tenth of 300.

items.stem: Put these in order to grow your training safely.

options.text: Pick a move you can do with good form.
options.feedback: A move you can do well gives a safe task to repeat and build on.

options.text: Repeat it until it feels easy.
options.feedback: Repeating the same work lets the body adapt, so it starts to feel easy.

options.text: Add a small amount of weight, reps or days.
options.feedback: Once it feels easy, a small rise gives the muscles a new task to adapt to.

misconceptions.name: More weight every visit
misconceptions.correction: A gradual rise can use clean reps, load or days; every visit need not be harder.

misconceptions.name: Bigger jumps work faster
misconceptions.correction: The size of each weekly jump, next to your usual amount, is linked to injury risk.

misconceptions.name: Nothing changed
misconceptions.correction: When the same work starts to feel easier, the body has adapted to it.

steps.title: Overload means asking a bit more than usual

hook.stem: Ten push-ups felt hard a month ago and feel easy now. What changed?

options.text: Your muscles got used to the work.
options.feedback: Right. Muscles adapt to work they are not used to, so the same task now feels easier.
The push-ups weigh the same as before. Your body changed, so the task takes less effort.

options.text: Easy now means you are getting weaker.
options.feedback: Easier means stronger here. Your muscles adapted to the load you kept giving them.

steps.teach: Muscles get stronger when you ask them to do a bit more than they are used to. This is called overload.

parts: Meera usually does 8 squats in her hostel room,
today she does 10 with the same good form,
and in a few weeks 10 will feel normal.
example.spot: today she does 10 with the same good form,
example.feedback: Two more squats than usual is the overload. Her legs then adapt to it.

guided.stem: Which of these asks the muscles for more than usual?
guided.hint: Look for a change from the normal routine.

options.text: Two more reps than last week.
options.feedback: Yes. Doing more than last week is overload.

options.text: The same set as every day.
options.feedback: The same set is work the body already knows, so it adds nothing new.
Skipping gives the muscle no work at all, so there is nothing to adapt to.

guided.stem: Rahul's 5 kg curls felt hard in his first week and feel easy now. What does that show?
guided.hint: Easy means the body has caught up.

options.text: His arms adapted to the load.
options.feedback: Right. The load used to be hard, and his arms grew able to handle it.
The dumbbell is still 5 kg. His arms are what changed.

options.text: He must be doing them wrong.
options.feedback: Feeling easier over weeks is a normal sign of adapting, not of bad form.

steps.takeaway: Muscles adapt when you ask a little more than usual.

steps.title: Keep progress going: add weight, reps or days

hook.stem: Your 10 squats feel easy now. What could make them a fresh challenge?

options.text: Add a few clean reps or hold a weight.
options.feedback: Right. More clean reps or a little weight gives the muscle a new task.

options.text: Do the same 10, faster and sloppier.
options.feedback: Sloppy reps do not add useful work. Clean extra reps or weight do.

options.text: Nothing, since easy means you are done.
options.feedback: Easy means you have adapted. A small new challenge keeps progress going.

steps.teach: To keep getting stronger, the work has to grow. You can add weight, add clean reps, or add a training day each week.

parts: Kabir did strength work twice a week last term,
then added a third day this term,
and his lifts kept getting stronger.
example.spot: then added a third day this term,
example.feedback: Adding a training day raised his weekly work, so his strength kept rising.

guided.stem: Sana can do 12 clean lunges. Which change grows the work?

options.text: Hold a water bottle in each hand.
options.feedback: Yes. The bottles add a little weight, so each lunge is a bit harder.

options.text: Do 12 lunges at half the depth.
options.feedback: Shallow lunges make each rep easier, so the work shrinks instead of growing.
Fewer reps is less work, not more, so it will not push her further.

guided.stem: Two friends lift the same today. One adds a little weight each month; one never changes. Who is likely stronger in a year?
guided.hint: The guide links more weight to stronger muscles.

options.feedback: Right. A rising load keeps giving the muscles something new to adapt to.
Doing the same work keeps giving the same task, so it adds less over time.
Their work differs. Adding weight over time builds more strength.

steps.takeaway: To keep improving, add weight, clean reps or a training day.

steps.title: Keep each weekly jump small

hook.stem: Who takes the bigger jump: going from 40 to 60 minutes a week, or from 200 to 220?

options.feedback: Right. 20 more minutes is a 50% jump on 40, but only 10% on 200.
Both add 20 minutes, but 20 on top of 200 is only a 10% rise.
The minutes match, but the share does not. 20 is half of 40.

steps.teach: Grow the work in small steps. How big each weekly jump is, next to what you already do, is linked to injury risk.

parts: Isha jogs 100 minutes a week,
adds just 10 minutes the next week,
and keeps that new total for a while.
example.spot: adds just 10 minutes the next week,
example.feedback: Ten minutes on top of 100 is a 10% rise, a small step for her body.

guided.stem: Ravi runs 50 minutes a week. Which next week is the smallest jump for him?
guided.hint: Compare each rise with his usual 50 minutes.

options.feedback: Yes. 5 more on 50 is a 10% rise, a gentle step.
25 more on 50 is a 50% rise, a big jump for one week.
Doubling to 100 is a 100% rise, far bigger than the other choices.

guided.stem: Why do beginners need extra care with big jumps?
guided.hint: Compare the jump with their usual amount.

options.text: When you do little, any jump is a big share.
options.feedback: Right. Starting from a small amount, even a few extra minutes is a large rise.
Beginners can gain a lot. They just need jumps that are small for them.

options.text: Big jumps are fine for everyone.
options.feedback: The guide links the size of each jump to injury risk, for everyone.

steps.takeaway: Keep each weekly jump small next to what you already do.

concepts.title: Muscle, protein and rest
concepts.hook: Training gives muscle a task. Food and time between hard sessions help the body respond.
concepts.rule: Strength work is the signal to build and protein is the material. Most who exercise do well on 1.4 to 2.0 g per kilo a day, and building can go on for up to 48 hours after a session.

claims.text: The ISSN stand gives about 1.4 to 2.0 grams of protein per kilogram per day for most exercising people.
Strength work and eating protein both switch on muscle building, and together they do more than either alone.
The ISSN suggests about 20 to 40 grams of protein per meal, spread every 3 to 4 hours.
After one strength session, muscle building can stay raised for up to 48 hours.

items.stem: Match each part to its job in building muscle.

options.feedback: Lifting or push-ups give the muscle a hard task, which is the signal to build.
The signal comes from training, which tells the muscle to start building.
Dal, curd, eggs or paneer bring protein that the body can use after training.
Protein from food supplies the parts the muscle uses to build.

items.stem: In the college hostel, Sid drinks two protein shakes a day but skips every workout. What is most likely?

options.text: Less muscle building than if he trained too.
options.feedback: Protein and strength work boost building together. Without training, he gets less of it.

options.text: As much muscle as a regular lifter.
options.feedback: Shakes cannot replace the training signal, so he builds less than a lifter.

options.text: Twice the muscle building from two shakes.
options.feedback: More shakes do not double building. The missing piece is the training.

items.stem: In a review, people did a strength session before eating anything. What happened to their muscle building?

options.text: It still rose after the session.
options.feedback: The review found muscle building rose after strength work even in people who had not eaten.

options.text: It stayed flat until they ate.
options.feedback: It rose without food too. Training on its own is a signal to build.
It went up, not down. The session itself raised muscle building.

items.stem: To support muscle building, about how many grams of protein per meal does the ISSN stand suggest?

options.feedback: The stand suggests 20 to 40 grams per meal, so 30 sits in the middle.
5 grams is well below the stand's 20 to 40 grams per meal.
100 grams is far above the 20 to 40 grams the stand gives per meal.

items.stem: Priya weighs 55 kg, runs for her college team and eats about 45 grams of protein a day. How does that compare with the stand?

options.text: Below her range of about 77 to 110 grams.
options.feedback: 55 times 1.4 is 77, so 45 grams sits well under the low end.
Her range starts at 77 grams, so 45 grams is under it.
Above would mean more than 110 grams. 45 grams is far below that.

items.stem: A friend says eating a whole day's protein in one dinner works just as well. What is missing?

options.text: The stand suggests doses spread through the day.
options.feedback: The stand suggests 20 to 40 grams per meal, spread every 3 to 4 hours.
No meal time is magic. The stand suggests even doses spread through the day.
Dinner protein is digested fine. The point is spreading doses, not the time.

items.stem: Which line best explains why rest days are part of training?

options.text: Muscle keeps building for up to two days after a session.
options.feedback: A review found muscle building can stay raised for up to 48 hours after one session.

options.text: Muscles only grow while you lift.
options.feedback: Building goes on after you stop, for up to about 48 hours.
Rest days do not undo the work. Building carries on during them.

items.stem: A review found a smaller rise in muscle building for adults over 50 than for those under 35. Why is one rule for everyone a problem?

options.text: The response differs with age and how hard the session is.
options.feedback: The review found age and the session's load both changed how big the rise was.

options.text: Adults over 50 build no muscle at all.
options.feedback: They still had a rise, just a smaller one than younger adults.

options.text: The review only looked at food.
options.feedback: The review looked at strength sessions themselves, measured before any meal.

misconceptions.name: One part is enough
misconceptions.correction: Training, food protein and time each play a part in muscle change.

misconceptions.name: All at once is the same
misconceptions.correction: The stand suggests 20 to 40 grams per meal, spread every 3 to 4 hours.

misconceptions.name: Growth happens only in the gym
misconceptions.correction: Muscle building can stay raised for up to 48 hours after a session.

steps.title: Training is the signal, protein is the material

hook.stem: Two friends eat the same dal and paneer. Only one also does strength work. Whose muscles get the bigger boost?

options.feedback: Right. Training and protein work together, so doing both gives more muscle building.

options.text: Both the same, since the food is the same.
options.feedback: Food alone helps less. Strength work adds the signal that tells muscle to build.
Skipping training removes the signal to build. Protein works best next to the work.

steps.teach: Strength work tells muscle to build. Protein from food gives it the parts. Each helps alone, but they do more together.

parts: Ananya does squats and push-ups at 6 pm,
then eats rajma, rice and curd for dinner,
and sleeps well that night.
example.spot: Ananya does squats and push-ups at 6 pm,
example.feedback: The squats and push-ups are the signal. The meal then brings the parts to build with.

guided.stem: Kiran drinks a protein shake daily but never trains. What is he missing?
guided.hint: Food is one half of the pair.

options.feedback: Yes. Protein helps most next to strength work, which gives the signal to build.
More protein cannot stand in for training. The signal to build is what is missing.
Protein helps, but the stand says it works best together with exercise.

guided.stem: In the pair, what role does protein play?
guided.hint: One part is the signal, one part is the material.

options.feedback: Right. Protein supplies the parts that muscle is built from.

options.text: It is the signal to grow.
options.feedback: Training is the signal. Protein supplies the parts that muscle builds from.

options.text: It replaces the need to train.
options.feedback: Protein cannot replace the work. It adds parts once training gives the signal.

steps.takeaway: Training gives the signal; protein gives the parts.

steps.title: How much protein, and how often

hook.stem: About how much protein a day suits a 60 kg person who exercises?

options.feedback: Right. At 1.4 to 2.0 grams per kilo, 60 kg works out to about 84 to 120 grams.
That is far too little. Even the low end is 1.4 grams for each kilo.
That is far too much. The range is 1.4 to 2.0 grams per kilo a day.

steps.teach: Most people who exercise do well on 1.4 to 2.0 grams of protein per kilo of body weight a day. Times your weight gives your range.

visual.label: Protein per kilo a day, most who exercise

parts: Rohit weighs 50 kg and lifts weights,
so about 70 to 100 grams of protein a day fits the stand,
spread over his meals.
example.spot: so about 70 to 100 grams of protein a day fits the stand,
example.feedback: 50 times 1.4 is 70 and 50 times 2.0 is 100, so his range is 70 to 100 grams.

guided.stem: Meena weighs 70 kg and trains. What is the low end of her daily range?

options.feedback: Yes. 70 times 1.4 is 98 grams a day.
That uses 1 gram per kilo. The low end of the range is 1.4 grams per kilo.
That is 70 times 2.0, the high end, not the low end.

guided.stem: The stand suggests 20 to 40 grams per meal, every 3 to 4 hours. Which day fits best?
guided.hint: Look for even meals, spread out.

options.text: Four meals of about 25 grams each, spread out.
options.feedback: Yes. Four even meals of 25 grams sit inside the range and are spread through the day.

options.text: One meal of 100 grams at night.
options.feedback: One big meal puts it all at once. The stand suggests doses every 3 to 4 hours.
5 grams at a time is well below the 20 to 40 grams per meal the stand gives.

steps.takeaway: For most who exercise: 1.4 to 2.0 g protein per kilo a day.

steps.title: Building goes on after the session

hook.stem: After a hard strength session, how long can muscle building stay raised?

options.feedback: Right. A review found it can stay raised for up to 48 hours after one session.
Building goes on well after the session ends, for up to about two days.
A month is far too long. The review found up to about 48 hours.

steps.teach: Building muscle goes on after a session ends. One hard session can keep it raised for up to two days, so rest time counts too.

parts: Zoya trains her legs on Monday evening,
her muscles keep building through Tuesday,
and she trains her arms on Wednesday.
example.spot: her muscles keep building through Tuesday,
example.feedback: Muscle building can stay raised for up to 48 hours after one session.

guided.stem: Dev trains at 6 pm. Until about when can muscle building stay raised?

options.feedback: Yes. 48 hours after 6 pm lands at 6 pm two days later.
One hour is far too short. It can stay raised for up to 48 hours.
A week is much longer than the 48 hours the review found.

guided.stem: Which line about the 48 hours is true?

options.text: It can last up to 48 hours, and it varies.
options.feedback: Right. The review found up to 48 hours, with big differences between studies.
Not always. The time and size of the rise varied a lot between studies.
The rise starts soon after the session ends, not two days later.

steps.takeaway: Muscle building can stay raised for up to two days after training.

concepts.title: Sleep and recovery
concepts.hook: A late exam night can make the next run feel harder and the canteen snack more tempting.
concepts.rule: Adults are advised 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night. Short sleep can lower sports performance and make you hungrier. The size of the effect differs between people.

claims.text: Adults are advised to get about 7 to 9 hours of sleep; sleep loss can harm exercise output and hunger cues.
Experts advise adults to sleep 7 to 9 hours a night, and teens aged 13 to 18 to sleep 8 to 10 hours.
In a review of athletes, one night of short sleep lowered sports performance. Losing the last part of the night hurt most.
With too little sleep, the hunger hormone ghrelin goes up and the fullness hormone leptin goes down, so you feel hungrier.

items.stem: A student sleeps 6 hours a night. About how many more hours of sleep would reach the low end of the adult range?

options.feedback: The adult range starts at 7 hours, so 6 needs about 1 more.
3 more would make 9, the top of the range, not the low end.
6 hours is under the 7 advised for adults, so some more is needed.

items.stem: For teens aged 13 to 18, the advised sleep is ___ hours a day.

options.feedback: Teens are advised 8 to 10 hours, a bit more than the 7 to 9 for adults.
That is short even for adults. Teens are advised 8 to 10.
That is more than advised for teens. Their range is 8 to 10.

items.stem: A friend says sleep is just downtime, so it plays no part in training. What is wrong?

options.text: Sleep helps the body recover from training.
options.feedback: Sleep helps the body bounce back. Short sleep can hurt your game and make you hungrier.

options.text: Sleep only matters for the brain.
options.feedback: Sleep helps the brain, but it also aids body recovery and steady hunger.

options.text: Training goes better with less sleep.
options.feedback: Studies of athletes find short sleep lowers performance, not raises it.

items.stem: Before a cricket match, Arjun sleeps at his usual time but wakes at 4 am for the bus. What is likely?

options.text: His play may drop, since the early wake cut his sleep.
options.feedback: Cutting sleep at the end of the night hit sport hardest in the review.

options.text: His play will improve from extra time awake.
options.feedback: Extra hours awake do not help. Short sleep tends to lower sports performance.
The review looked at a single night of short sleep and still found a drop.

items.stem: After short sleep, order these from biggest drop to smallest, as the review found.

options.feedback: Short bursts of hard effort with rests dropped the most in the review.
This dropped less than stop-start effort but more than explosive power.
Explosive power showed the smallest drop of these three.

items.stem: After a short night, Dev races at 9 am and Ria races at 4 pm. Who likely shows the bigger drop?

options.feedback: After short sleep, the review found a bigger drop in the afternoon than in the morning.
The morning drop was the smaller one. Afternoon performance fell more.

options.text: Neither, since one night does not matter.
options.feedback: One night was enough for a drop in the review, and it was bigger later in the day.

items.stem: Ghrelin and leptin both shift after short sleep. Which pair of changes adds up to more hunger?

options.feedback: Ghrelin drives hunger and leptin signals fullness, so this pair means more hunger.
That pair would mean less hunger. Short sleep does the opposite.
They move in opposite ways: ghrelin rises while leptin falls.

items.stem: In exam week, Sana sleeps 5 hours a night in the hostel and keeps raiding the canteen. Which change goes after the cause?

options.text: Getting closer to 7 to 9 hours of sleep.
options.feedback: Her short sleep is pushing ghrelin up and leptin down, so more sleep tackles the cause.

options.text: Skipping lunch to make up for snacks.
options.feedback: Skipping meals does not touch the cause. The short sleep is what shifts her hunger signals.
Later nights cut sleep further, which would push her hunger up even more.

misconceptions.name: Sleep is separate from training
misconceptions.correction: Sleep can shape rest, sport and hunger cues.

misconceptions.name: Any amount of sleep is enough
misconceptions.correction: Adults are advised 7 to 9 hours a night, and teens 8 to 10.

misconceptions.name: Tired play is the same play
misconceptions.correction: In a review of athletes, one short night tended to lower sports performance.

steps.title: How much sleep the body needs

hook.stem: How much sleep a night do experts advise for adults?

options.feedback: Right. Experts advise adults to sleep 7 to 9 hours a night.
That is well under the advice. Adults are advised 7 to 9 hours.
That is more than advised. The range for adults is 7 to 9 hours.

steps.teach: Sleep is part of training, not a break from it. Adults are advised 7 to 9 hours a night. Teens need 8 to 10.

parts: Aman sleeps 8 hours on most nights,
but only 5 hours before his exam,
and his morning run feels heavy.
example.spot: but only 5 hours before his exam,
example.feedback: 5 hours is well under the 7 to 9 hours advised for adults.

guided.stem: A 16-year-old sleeps 7 hours a night. How does that fit the advice for teens?
guided.hint: Teens 13 to 18 are advised 8 to 10 hours.

options.text: It is a bit under the teen range.
options.feedback: Yes. 7 hours is just short of the 8 to 10 advised for teens.

options.text: It is right in the middle.
options.feedback: The teen range is 8 to 10 hours, so 7 is below it.

options.text: It is more than teens need.
options.feedback: 7 hours sits under the teen range of 8 to 10, not above it.

guided.stem: Rhea sleeps from 1 am to 7 am. Is she in the adult range?

options.feedback: Right. 1 am to 7 am is 6 hours, one short of the low end.
The adult range starts at 7 hours, so 6 falls short.
The advice is about hours. 6 is short of the 7 to 9 advised.

steps.takeaway: Adults: 7 to 9 hours a night. Teens: 8 to 10.

steps.title: Short sleep drags down your game

hook.stem: You slept badly before a big match. What do you guess happens to your game?

options.feedback: Right. A review of athletes found one short night lowers performance.
Short sleep tends to hurt play, not help it, in studies of athletes.

options.text: Sleep makes no difference to sport.
options.feedback: The review found a clear drop in performance after short sleep.

steps.teach: One bad night can drag down your game. In studies of athletes, waking far too early hurt more than going to bed late.

parts: Kunal went to bed at his usual time,
but woke at 4 am for a long train trip,
and his badminton was off that evening.
example.spot: but woke at 4 am for a long train trip,
example.feedback: Cutting sleep at the end of the night hit sport hardest in the review.

guided.stem: Which short-sleep pattern hurt sport most in the review?
guided.hint: Think about when in the night sleep was cut.

options.text: Waking up much earlier than usual.
options.feedback: Yes. Losing the end of the night showed the biggest drop.

options.text: Going to bed a bit late, then sleeping in.
options.feedback: Losing the start of the night showed no clear effect in the review.
A full night is no sleep loss at all, so there is nothing to hurt.

guided.stem: Which line best fits what the review found?

options.text: One short night can lower sports performance.
options.feedback: Yes. Even a single short night lowered athletes' overall performance.

options.text: It takes a month of short sleep to matter.
options.feedback: The review looked at one night of short sleep and still found a drop.
Speed dropped after short sleep too, so it did not help.

steps.takeaway: Short sleep, most of all an early wake, can drag down sport.

steps.title: Short sleep turns up hunger

hook.stem: Why might you crave snacks after a short night?

options.feedback: Right. Ghrelin goes up and leptin goes down, so you feel hungrier.

options.text: You burned lots of energy sleeping.
options.feedback: It is not about energy burned. Hunger hormones shift when sleep is short.
